# Industry-Based Modern Design Strategy & Free Library/CDN Catalog
<!-- id: design.industry-based-modern-design-strategy-and-free-library-cdn-catalog -->

Version: 2026-08-09

Purpose: A modern design-strategy reference for websites, apps, portals, marketplaces, dashboards, and SaaS products across the full industry taxonomy.

> This document is a design and implementation reference, not a requirement to use every listed pattern or dependency. Validate each design against user needs, performance, accessibility, privacy, security, business model, content strategy, and device context.

# Modern Design Principles
<!-- id: design.modern-design-principles -->

- Design from user journeys and information priority, not from visual trends.
- Use a tokenized design system for typography, spacing, color, radius, elevation, motion, breakpoints, and semantic states.
- Prefer responsive container-based composition and content-driven breakpoints over device-specific layouts.
- Use modern CSS capabilities where browser support fits the audience: grid, flexbox, container queries, logical properties, `clamp()`, aspect-ratio, CSS variables, and progressive enhancement.
- Build strong typography hierarchy before adding decoration.
- Use cards only when content is meaningfully modular; avoid wrapping every element in a card.
- Use bento layouts selectively for heterogeneous modules, not as a universal homepage pattern.
- Use glass, blur, glow, gradients, and noise as accents—not as substitutes for hierarchy or contrast.
- Use dark mode when it improves the task or audience fit; do not force dark mode as a symbol of modernity.
- Use motion to communicate continuity, state, hierarchy, causality, or delight; respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Use 3D only when spatial understanding, configuration, inspection, storytelling, or brand experience materially benefits.
- Make mobile layouts task-specific rather than simply stacking desktop sections.
- Keep touch targets large, controls keyboard-operable, and focus states visible.
- Never convey status or meaning by color alone.
- Preserve semantic HTML and text alternatives even in highly visual experiences.
- Keep primary content available without JavaScript where practical for resilient public content sites.
- Design empty, loading, error, offline, permission, and destructive states as part of the system.
- Optimize real images, video, fonts, charts, and third-party scripts as aggressively as layout code.
- Maintain visual consistency between marketing, product, documentation, support, and legal surfaces.

# Modern Visual System Baseline
<!-- id: design.modern-visual-system-baseline -->

## Typography

- Use one primary text family and at most one contrasting display family unless the brand system has a deliberate reason for more.
- Prefer variable fonts when they reduce requests and provide useful weight/width ranges.
- Maintain comfortable body line length, generally around 45–80 characters depending on context.
- Use fluid type with bounded `clamp()` values rather than extreme viewport scaling.
- Use tabular numerals for financial, scientific, sports, logistics, and operational data where supported.

## Spacing

- Use a consistent spacing scale such as 4/8-based tokens.
- Increase macro whitespace for editorial/luxury contexts; increase information density for operational and technical contexts.
- Use whitespace to establish grouping before adding borders, shadows, or containers.

## Color

- Define semantic tokens for background, surface, text, muted text, border, primary action, success, warning, danger, and information.
- Support light/dark schemes only when both can meet contrast and content-quality requirements.
- Use brand color as a system, not a single hex value applied indiscriminately.

## Radius and Elevation

- Choose a radius family that reflects brand character; avoid mixing every available radius size on one page.
- Use elevation only to indicate layering or interaction depth.
- Prefer borders, tonal surfaces, and spacing over heavy drop shadows for dense professional interfaces.

## Motion

- Favor transform and opacity for performant motion.
- Keep common UI transitions short and purposeful.
- Avoid scroll-jacking.
- Provide reduced-motion alternatives.
- Do not animate continuously without user or task benefit.

# CDN & Dependency Production Standards
<!-- id: design.cdn-and-dependency-production-standards -->

- Pin exact tested versions in production instead of `latest` or broad ranges.
- Prefer package-managed, bundled, and tree-shaken production builds for substantial applications.
- Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) when supported and practical for classic CDN scripts/styles.
- Define a Content Security Policy appropriate to the application and selected CDNs.
- Self-host critical assets when reliability, privacy, compliance, or performance warrants it.
- Review licenses before commercial distribution and before bundling assets into redistributed products.
- Remember that an open-source map library does not make map tiles, geocoding, imagery, or place data free.
- Avoid loading multiple libraries that solve the same problem.
- Measure third-party impact on Core Web Vitals and bundle size.
- Lazy-load heavy visualization, map, carousel, and 3D code when it is below the fold or task-specific.
- Do not use Tailwind's Play CDN in production; the official documentation labels it development-only.

# Verified Free/Open Design & Interaction Toolkit
<!-- id: design.verified-free-open-design-and-interaction-toolkit -->

## Tailwind CSS

- Best for: utility-first CSS and design tokens
- Official: https://tailwindcss.com/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@tailwindcss/browser@4`
- Note: Play CDN is for development only; use a compiled production build.

## Bootstrap 5.3

- Best for: responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components
- Official: https://getbootstrap.com/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.8/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css`
- Note: Production-ready CDN builds are documented by Bootstrap.

## htmx

- Best for: HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework
- Official: https://htmx.org/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/htmx.org@2.0.10/dist/htmx.min.js`
- Note: Good for server-rendered portals, search, filters, forms, and partial updates.

## Alpine.js

- Best for: lightweight client-side UI state and interactions
- Official: https://alpinejs.dev/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/alpinejs/dist/cdn.min.js`
- Note: Pin a tested version for production.

## Swiper

- Best for: touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders
- Official: https://swiperjs.com/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/swiper@12/swiper-bundle.min.js`
- Note: Use only when a carousel is genuinely useful; avoid hiding primary content.

## Chart.js

- Best for: accessible-minded common charts and dashboards
- Official: https://www.chartjs.org/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js`
- Note: Pin a version in production; provide textual/table equivalents for critical data.

## Apache ECharts

- Best for: advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization
- Official: https://echarts.apache.org/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/echarts/dist/echarts.min.js`
- Note: Available through free CDNs including jsDelivr, unpkg, and cdnjs.

## D3

- Best for: custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics
- Official: https://d3js.org/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/d3@7/+esm`
- Note: Best when standard chart libraries cannot express the required visualization.

## Leaflet

- Best for: lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps
- Official: https://leafletjs.com/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js`
- Note: 1.9.4 is the documented stable release; map tile/data providers have separate terms.

## MapLibre GL JS

- Best for: open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers
- Official: https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl.js`
- Note: The library is open source; map styles, tiles, geocoding, and datasets may have separate costs/licenses.

## three.js

- Best for: 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences
- Official: https://threejs.org/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@<pinned-version>/build/three.module.js`
- Note: Use import maps/modules and pin the same version for core and addons.

## Motion

- Best for: production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL
- Official: https://motion.dev/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/motion@<pinned-version>/+esm`
- Note: Core Motion is free/open source; some Motion+ features are paid. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

## Anime.js

- Best for: lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation
- Official: https://animejs.com/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/animejs/dist/bundles/anime.umd.min.js`
- Note: Use motion as enhancement, not as a requirement to understand or operate the interface.

## Lucide

- Best for: consistent scalable SVG icons
- Official: https://lucide.dev/
- CDN / delivery example: `Package/framework integration preferred`
- Note: Released under the ISC License according to the official Lucide site.

## FullCalendar

- Best for: calendar, schedule, agenda, and event interfaces
- Official: https://fullcalendar.io/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/fullcalendar@7.0.2/all/global.js`
- Note: Use the standard/free bundle for core calendar views; scheduler/resource features may be premium.

## Google Fonts

- Best for: large catalog of web typography
- Official: https://fonts.google.com/
- CDN / delivery example: `https://fonts.googleapis.com/`
- Note: For privacy/performance-sensitive projects, consider self-hosting licensed font files instead of third-party loading.

# Library Selection Guide
<!-- id: design.library-selection-guide -->

| Need | Recommended starting point |
|---|---|
| Utility-first CSS/design tokens | Tailwind CSS compiled build |
| Traditional responsive component framework | Bootstrap 5.3 |
| HTML-first partial page interactions | htmx |
| Lightweight local UI state | Alpine.js |
| Touch galleries/carousels | Swiper |
| Common charts | Chart.js |
| Advanced dashboards / large visualization | Apache ECharts |
| Bespoke visualization | D3 |
| Lightweight raster/tile maps | Leaflet |
| Vector maps / globe / 3D terrain | MapLibre GL JS |
| 3D product/scene experiences | three.js |
| Modern UI/SVG/scroll animation | Motion |
| Timeline/SVG/text animation | Anime.js |
| SVG icon system | Lucide |
| Calendar/schedule interfaces | FullCalendar standard bundle |
| Web typography catalog | Google Fonts or self-hosted licensed fonts |

# Design Anti-Patterns
<!-- id: design.design-anti-patterns -->

- Do not use glassmorphism everywhere.
- Do not use giant rounded cards as the default container for every content block.
- Do not hide navigation behind a hamburger menu on wide desktop screens without a strong reason.
- Do not use autoplay carousels for critical information.
- Do not use horizontal scroll for ordinary desktop content.
- Do not use scroll-jacking or fake smooth-scroll that harms keyboard, anchor, or assistive behavior.
- Do not use low-contrast gray text simply to look minimal.
- Do not use excessive gradients, blobs, mesh backgrounds, or glows without brand purpose.
- Do not use 3D charts for conventional quantitative comparison.
- Do not replace text labels with icons when the icon meaning is not universal.
- Do not use hover as the only way to discover functionality.
- Do not make mobile users dismiss multiple overlays before seeing content.
- Do not animate layout in ways that cause unexpected movement around forms or reading content.
- Do not add a library solely because it is fashionable.

# Industry Mapping
<!-- id: design.industry-mapping -->

# Agriculture & Farming
<!-- id: design.industry.agriculture-and-farming -->

**Design profile:** Agriculture  
**Operating profile:** Agriculture  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Agriculture & Farming** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Agriculture & Farming.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Crop Production, Grain Farming, Fruit & Vegetable Farming, Greenhouse & Nursery Production, Livestock Farming.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use grounded, high-clarity interfaces combining field imagery, operational data, weather, traceability, and product information.
- Design for outdoor/mobile use with high contrast, large controls, and intermittent connectivity assumptions where applicable.
- Use maps for fields, service regions, logistics, and asset location.
- Use charts for yield, moisture, weather, pricing, and production trends with explicit units.
- Favor authentic photography and technical diagrams over generic pastoral imagery.
- Keep workflows task-centered for growers, buyers, operators, and advisors.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Low-contrast earth-tone interfaces
- Map-only field data
- Desktop-first tables unusable outdoors
- Decorative sustainability badges without evidence

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Mining & Natural Resources
<!-- id: design.industry.mining-and-natural-resources -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Manufacturing  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Mining & Natural Resources** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Mining & Natural Resources.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Coal Mining, Metal Mining, Gold Mining, Silver Mining, Copper Mining.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Construction** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Construction.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Residential Construction, Commercial Construction, Industrial Construction, Civil Engineering, Infrastructure Construction.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use project- and capability-first layouts with strong grids, market/service hierarchy, project proof, bid/RFQ actions, safety/quality evidence, and controlled document access.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use real project/site photography, progress imagery, plans, BIM/technical diagrams, logistics/site context, and finished-work evidence instead of generic hard-hat stock.
- Keep schedules, project facts, bid packages, RFIs/submittals, qualifications, and document indexes highly scannable with clear status and ownership.
- Use BIM/3D, maps, phasing, or site visualization only when it improves spatial understanding, coordination, constructability, or project communication.
- Design mobile for field lookup, project contacts, plans/documents, issue capture, approvals, photos, and fast escalation rather than reproducing every desktop view.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

# Retail
<!-- id: design.industry.retail -->

**Design profile:** Commerce  
**Operating profile:** Retail  
**Product profile:** Commerce

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Retail** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Retail.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Department Stores, Supermarkets, Grocery Stores, Convenience Stores, Clothing Stores.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a product-first visual system with large, crisp imagery, restrained chrome, and strong hierarchy around price, availability, variants, and primary purchase actions.
- Favor modular card grids, comparison states, sticky purchase controls, progressive disclosure, and fast faceted navigation.
- Use editorial storytelling selectively for premium collections, launches, and category education rather than turning every page into a campaign.
- Design mobile product pages around thumb reach, sticky actions, clear variant selection, and minimal checkout friction.
- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Autoplay carousels above the primary product information
- Low-contrast luxury styling that hides price or actions
- Overloaded mega-menus without search/filter support
- Motion-heavy checkout flows

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Financial Services** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.

- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks

- Ambiguous transaction buttons

# Information Technology
<!-- id: design.industry.information-technology -->

**Design profile:** Software  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Information Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Information Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: IT Services, Managed IT Services, Systems Integration, Computer Repair, Network Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

- Every surface using glassmorphism

- Overanimated dashboards

# Artificial Intelligence
<!-- id: design.industry.artificial-intelligence -->

**Design profile:** Ai  
**Operating profile:** Ai  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Artificial Intelligence** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Artificial Intelligence.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Generative AI, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, Computer Vision, AI Infrastructure.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Design around input → context → generation → review → action, making system state and user control explicit.
- Use conversational UI only where conversation is genuinely the best interaction model; provide structured controls for repeatable workflows.
- Separate user input, source context, AI output, citations, tool actions, and system status visually.
- Make uncertainty, limitations, provenance, and human review states legible without overwhelming the main task.
- Use streaming, progress, skeletons, and tool-call status carefully so latency feels understandable rather than mysterious.
- Use modern motion and ambient visual identity sparingly; clarity of output is more important than futuristic styling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Generic glowing-orb AI branding as the main interface
- Hiding sources or tool actions
- Typing animations that slow expert users
- Anthropomorphic UI that misrepresents autonomy

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Cybersecurity
<!-- id: design.industry.cybersecurity -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Cybersecurity** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Cybersecurity.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Network Security, Endpoint Security, Cloud Security, Application Security, Identity Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.
- Use charts and topology visuals carefully, with drill-down and textual evidence.
- Show trust evidence—controls, certifications, response process—without turning every page into a badge wall.
- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

- Green-code hacker clichés

# Telecommunications
<!-- id: design.industry.telecommunications -->

**Design profile:** Telecom  
**Operating profile:** Telecom  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Telecommunications** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Telecommunications.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Wireless Carriers, Fixed-Line Telecom, Broadband, Fiber Networks, Satellite Communications.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use comparison-first layouts for plans, coverage, devices, usage, and account actions.
- Make plan differences explicit with stable comparison tables and total recurring cost.
- Use maps for coverage/availability with text/address search alternatives.
- Use status modules for outages, activation, usage, billing, and device state.
- Keep technical network terminology translated into user outcomes.
- Use restrained brand motion; account and support flows should be fast and utilitarian.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Decorative 5G animations over plan details
- Coverage maps without disclaimers/legend
- Hidden fees
- Oversized plan cards that prevent comparison

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **HealthTech** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for HealthTech.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Telemedicine, Digital Health, Electronic Health Records, Healthcare Software, Remote Patient Monitoring.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a calm, accessible application system with predictable navigation, clear data states, strong role separation, and low cognitive load.
- Prioritize the actual clinical, administrative, research, or patient workflow supported by the product; do not invent appointment/provider/insurance flows unless the product requires them.
- Design forms and high-impact actions with clear labels, progressive disclosure, validation, confirmation, and recoverability.
- Use domain imagery sparingly inside product UI; favor legible data, status, evidence, and task continuity.
- Keep safety, emergency/escalation, consent, data provenance, and decision-support limitations visually distinct where applicable.
- Use motion minimally and respect reduced-motion preferences by default.

- Treat **Waste Management** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Waste Management.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Waste Collection, Recycling, Hazardous Waste, Medical Waste, Industrial Waste.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Map-only dashboards
- Animation on continuously updating data
- Unlabeled status colors
- Oversized cards that reduce operational density

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use strong editorial typography, clear content hierarchy, rich metadata, and fast discovery.
- Design homepage modules around editorial priority rather than equal-card grids everywhere.
- Use sticky players, chaptering, transcripts, playlists, and save/follow controls where relevant.
- Apply motion to transitions, covers, and media states without interfering with reading.

- Build a visual system flexible enough for breaking news, evergreen features, video, audio, and live content.

- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Infinite visual noise
- Autoplay audio
- Content cards with no hierarchy
- Animations that shift reading position

- Treat **Subscription Services** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

- Treat **Construction Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Construction Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Construction Software, Building Information Modeling, Construction Robotics, Modular Construction, Prefabrication.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use project- and capability-first layouts with strong grids, market/service hierarchy, project proof, bid/RFQ actions, safety/quality evidence, and controlled document access.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use real project/site photography, progress imagery, plans, BIM/technical diagrams, logistics/site context, and finished-work evidence instead of generic hard-hat stock.
- Keep schedules, project facts, bid packages, RFIs/submittals, qualifications, and document indexes highly scannable with clear status and ownership.
- Use BIM/3D, maps, phasing, or site visualization only when it improves spatial understanding, coordination, constructability, or project communication.
- Design mobile for field lookup, project contacts, plans/documents, issue capture, approvals, photos, and fast escalation rather than reproducing every desktop view.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Loyalty & Rewards** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.

- Maintain a neutral visual system that can accommodate dense technical content without feeling institutional or dated.

# Scientific Services
<!-- id: design.industry.scientific-services -->

**Design profile:** Science  
**Operating profile:** Science  
**Product profile:** Scientific & Technical

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Scientific Services** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Scientific Services.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Laboratories, Research Institutes, Testing Services, Scientific Consulting.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use evidence-first information architecture with strong typographic hierarchy, technical diagrams, figures, tables, and reproducible data views.
- Keep visual ornament secondary to methods, results, provenance, and source clarity.
- Use modular research cards, filters, citations, dataset tables, and figure captions.
- Choose chart types for analytical accuracy rather than visual novelty.
- Use interactive exploration when it reveals patterns that static figures cannot.
- Maintain a neutral visual system that can accommodate dense technical content without feeling institutional or dated.

- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

# GovTech
<!-- id: design.industry.govtech -->

**Design profile:** Government  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **GovTech** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for GovTech.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Government Software, Civic Technology, Digital Government, Public Safety Technology.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use service-first, plain-language design with high contrast, stable navigation, and strong accessibility.
- Prioritize task completion: apply, pay, renew, report, find, contact, track.
- Use clear information architecture, service categories, eligibility summaries, required documents, and step-by-step forms.
- Use maps and data visualization only where they improve public understanding.
- Design for older devices, slower connections, keyboard navigation, zoom, and assistive technologies.
- Keep brand styling restrained so official status and content clarity dominate.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trend-driven low-contrast styling
- Unnecessary animation
- PDF-only core services
- Hidden contact/escalation paths

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.

# Debt Collection
<!-- id: design.industry.debt-collection -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Debt Collection** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Debt Collection.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Consumer Collections, Commercial Collections, Receivables Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/

- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Decorative 5G animations over plan details
- Coverage maps without disclaimers/legend
- Hidden fees
- Oversized plan cards that prevent comparison

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Digital Identity
<!-- id: design.industry.digital-identity -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Digital Identity** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Digital Identity.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Authentication, Biometrics, Identity Platforms, Credential Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.
- Use charts and topology visuals carefully, with drill-down and textual evidence.
- Show trust evidence—controls, certifications, response process—without turning every page into a badge wall.
- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

# Signage
<!-- id: design.industry.signage -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Manufacturing  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Signage** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Signage.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Digital Signage, Commercial Signs, Billboards, Wayfinding Systems.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.

4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.

# Experiential Marketing
<!-- id: design.industry.experiential-marketing -->

**Design profile:** Events  
**Operating profile:** Events  
**Product profile:** Event Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Experiential Marketing** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Experiential Marketing.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Brand Activations, Pop-Up Events, Field Marketing.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use event identity boldly while keeping date, place, agenda, registration, speakers, and ticket status immediately accessible.
- Design schedules for quick scanning, filtering, favorites, timezone handling, and mobile use.
- Use speaker/performer imagery consistently and create strong session hierarchy.
- Use motion for anticipation and transitions, not for core schedule interaction.
- Make venue maps, directions, accessibility, and check-in information event-day priorities.
- For hybrid events, integrate live status, stream access, transcripts, and replay cleanly.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **FullCalendar** — calendar, schedule, agenda, and event interfaces — https://fullcalendar.io/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

- Brand animation before event details
- Agenda PDFs as the only schedule

# Promotional Products

**Design profile:** Commerce  
**Operating profile:** Retail  
**Product profile:** Commerce

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Promotional Products** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Promotional Products.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Branded Merchandise, Corporate Gifts, Custom Apparel.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a product-first visual system with large, crisp imagery, restrained chrome, and strong hierarchy around price, availability, variants, and primary purchase actions.
- Favor modular card grids, comparison states, sticky purchase controls, progressive disclosure, and fast faceted navigation.
- Use editorial storytelling selectively for premium collections, launches, and category education rather than turning every page into a campaign.
- Design mobile product pages around thumb reach, sticky actions, clear variant selection, and minimal checkout friction.
- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

- Autoplay carousels above the primary product information

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Digital Signatures** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Electronic Signatures, Digital Contracting, Document Authentication.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use authoritative, restrained typography and strong information hierarchy.
- Prioritize practice areas, attorney expertise, jurisdictions, contact/intake, and trust proof.
- Use readable long-form layouts for articles, case analyses, and legal resources.
- Make disclaimers and jurisdiction limitations clear without visually overwhelming the page.
- Use restrained imagery and avoid clichés such as gavels unless context genuinely requires them.
- Keep motion minimal, functional, and professional.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Autonomous Vehicles** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use immersive media, crisp spec hierarchy, model/variant comparison, and confidence-building ownership information.

- Keep price, availability, key specs, and primary actions continuously discoverable.
- Use motion to communicate mechanical precision, state transitions, and model changes rather than generic parallax.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.

- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning

# Personal Finance
<!-- id: design.industry.personal-finance -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Personal Finance** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Personal Finance.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Budgeting Apps, Credit Monitoring, Financial Education, Money Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Pension Funds, Retirement Planning, Retirement Platforms.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use immersive media, crisp spec hierarchy, model/variant comparison, and confidence-building ownership information.
- Combine editorial hero storytelling with highly functional inventory, configuration, financing, and service interfaces.
- Use dark themes selectively for performance/luxury contexts, with accessible contrast and readable forms.
- Use 3D or 360-degree product visualization for meaningful inspection and configuration.
- Keep price, availability, key specs, and primary actions continuously discoverable.
- Use motion to communicate mechanical precision, state transitions, and model changes rather than generic parallax.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Full-screen video that blocks basic information
- Dark-on-dark controls
- Overly cinematic inventory browsing
- Hiding real prices behind excessive lead forms

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Equity Management

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Equity Management** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Cap Table Management, Employee Stock Plans, Shareholder Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Green Building** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Sustainable Construction, Building Efficiency, LEED Consulting.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use project- and capability-first layouts with strong grids, market/service hierarchy, project proof, bid/RFQ actions, safety/quality evidence, and controlled document access.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use real project/site photography, progress imagery, plans, BIM/technical diagrams, logistics/site context, and finished-work evidence instead of generic hard-hat stock.
- Keep schedules, project facts, bid packages, RFIs/submittals, qualifications, and document indexes highly scannable with clear status and ownership.
- Use BIM/3D, maps, phasing, or site visualization only when it improves spatial understanding, coordination, constructability, or project communication.
- Design mobile for field lookup, project contacts, plans/documents, issue capture, approvals, photos, and fast escalation rather than reproducing every desktop view.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Funeral Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Funeral Software, Memorial Platforms, Digital Legacy.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

- Use an editorial, art-directed layout with generous whitespace, disciplined typography, controlled asymmetry, and high-resolution media.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust commerce interface that balances product clarity, evidence, accessibility, and purchase efficiency without imitating a clinical portal.
- Prioritize product purpose, ingredients/materials, instructions, substantiated claims, warnings, price, availability, fulfillment, and support.

- Use motion for product-state feedback only; preserve fast, accessible shopping and reduced-motion support.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Clinical Genetics, Consumer Genetics, Genomic Testing.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use evidence-first information architecture with strong typographic hierarchy, technical diagrams, figures, tables, and reproducible data views.
- Keep visual ornament secondary to methods, results, provenance, and source clarity.
- Use modular research cards, filters, citations, dataset tables, and figure captions.
- Choose chart types for analytical accuracy rather than visual novelty.
- Use interactive exploration when it reveals patterns that static figures cannot.
- Maintain a neutral visual system that can accommodate dense technical content without feeling institutional or dated.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- 3D charts for 2D quantitative data
- Unlabeled axes
- Dashboard decoration that competes with evidence
- Color scales without accessible legends

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Confectionery** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Candy, Chocolate, Gum, Desserts.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/

# Hospitality Technology
<!-- id: design.industry.hospitality-technology -->

**Design profile:** Hospitality  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Hospitality Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Hospitality Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Hotel Software, Property Management Systems, Guest Experience Technology.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use a high-emotion editorial layer for property storytelling and a high-clarity transactional layer for rooms, rates, and policies.
- Design availability selectors, date pickers, occupancy controls, and rate cards for fast comparison.
- Use photography in consistent ratios and avoid galleries that trap users in modal loops.
- Create distinct visual hierarchy for room type, cancellation terms, included benefits, taxes, and total price.
- Use local-area maps and itinerary content to extend the property experience.
- Keep mobile booking controls sticky and reduce re-entry of dates/guests.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/

- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Brand videos before booking information
- Hidden rate conditions
- Overly decorative date pickers
- Low-contrast image overlays
