# Surveying
<!-- id: design.industry.surveying -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Construction  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Surveying** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Surveying.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Land Surveying, Construction Surveying, Geospatial Surveying.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use project- and capability-first layouts with strong grids, market/service hierarchy, project proof, bid/RFQ actions, safety/quality evidence, and controlled document access.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use real project/site photography, progress imagery, plans, BIM/technical diagrams, logistics/site context, and finished-work evidence instead of generic hard-hat stock.
- Keep schedules, project facts, bid packages, RFIs/submittals, qualifications, and document indexes highly scannable with clear status and ownership.
- Use BIM/3D, maps, phasing, or site visualization only when it improves spatial understanding, coordination, constructability, or project communication.
- Design mobile for field lookup, project contacts, plans/documents, issue capture, approvals, photos, and fast escalation rather than reproducing every desktop view.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Mortgage Technology
<!-- id: design.industry.mortgage-technology -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Mortgage Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Mortgage Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Digital Mortgages, Loan Origination Systems, Mortgage Data.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

- Treat **Home Electronics** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.

- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

2. Define design tokens and reusable components.

5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

# Mobile Devices
<!-- id: design.industry.mobile-devices -->

**Design profile:** Commerce  
**Operating profile:** Retail  
**Product profile:** Commerce

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Mobile Devices** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Mobile Devices.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a product-first visual system with large, crisp imagery, restrained chrome, and strong hierarchy around price, availability, variants, and primary purchase actions.
- Favor modular card grids, comparison states, sticky purchase controls, progressive disclosure, and fast faceted navigation.
- Use editorial storytelling selectively for premium collections, launches, and category education rather than turning every page into a campaign.
- Design mobile product pages around thumb reach, sticky actions, clear variant selection, and minimal checkout friction.
- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/

- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Autoplay carousels above the primary product information
- Low-contrast luxury styling that hides price or actions
- Overloaded mega-menus without search/filter support
- Motion-heavy checkout flows

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.

# Cash Management
<!-- id: design.industry.cash-management -->

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Logistics  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Cash Management** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Cash Management.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Cash Logistics, Armored Transportation, Cash Processing.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Map-only dashboards
- Animation on continuously updating data
- Unlabeled status colors
- Oversized cards that reduce operational density

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

# Fasteners
<!-- id: design.industry.fasteners -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Manufacturing  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Fasteners** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Fasteners.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Industrial Fasteners, Construction Fasteners.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Decorative green gradients as a substitute for evidence
- Unqualified sustainability visuals
- 3D charts
- Map layers without legends

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Marine Insurance
<!-- id: design.industry.marine-insurance -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Marine Insurance** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Marine Insurance.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Vessel Insurance, Cargo Insurance, Maritime Risk.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Marine Logistics
<!-- id: design.industry.marine-logistics -->

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Logistics  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Marine Logistics** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Marine Logistics.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Port Logistics, Vessel Logistics, Offshore Logistics.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

- Animation on continuously updating data

- Use custom diagrams and frameworks to make intellectual property visible.
- Keep service pages highly structured: problem, approach, evidence, deliverables, team, next step.
- Use subtle motion to improve polish without making the firm feel like a consumer app.
- Design long-form thought leadership for reading, citation, and sharing.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Generic stock-photo hero sections
- Excessive gradients
- Vague one-word service cards
- Overanimated consulting sites

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

**Operating profile:** Construction

- Treat **Rail Infrastructure** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.

- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

# Salvage

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Logistics

- Treat **Salvage** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Marine Salvage, Vehicle Salvage, Industrial Salvage.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.

- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

# Data Destruction
<!-- id: design.industry.data-destruction -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Data Destruction** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Data Destruction.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Secure Erasure, Physical Destruction, Records Destruction.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.
- Use charts and topology visuals carefully, with drill-down and textual evidence.
- Show trust evidence—controls, certifications, response process—without turning every page into a badge wall.
- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Green-code hacker clichés
- Glowing neon dashboards
- Severity conveyed by color alone
- Animated threat maps that distract from action

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.

# Supply Chain Traceability

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Logistics  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Supply Chain Traceability** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Supply Chain Traceability.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Product Tracking, Blockchain Traceability, Compliance Tracking.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

# Content Moderation

**Design profile:** Software  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Content Moderation** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Content Moderation.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Trust & Safety, Online Moderation, Community Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

# Email Security
<!-- id: design.industry.email-security -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Email Security** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Email Security.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Anti-Spam, Phishing Protection, Secure Email.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.
- Use charts and topology visuals carefully, with drill-down and textual evidence.
- Show trust evidence—controls, certifications, response process—without turning every page into a badge wall.
- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Green-code hacker clichés
- Glowing neon dashboards
- Severity conveyed by color alone
- Animated threat maps that distract from action

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Green-code hacker clichés
- Glowing neon dashboards
- Severity conveyed by color alone
- Animated threat maps that distract from action

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use strong editorial typography, clear content hierarchy, rich metadata, and fast discovery.
- Design homepage modules around editorial priority rather than equal-card grids everywhere.
- Use sticky players, chaptering, transcripts, playlists, and save/follow controls where relevant.
- Apply motion to transitions, covers, and media states without interfering with reading.
- Use dark mode when it improves long-form or media consumption, not as a mandatory brand signal.
- Build a visual system flexible enough for breaking news, evergreen features, video, audio, and live content.

- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/

- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/

- Infinite visual noise
- Autoplay audio

- Animations that shift reading position

# Earth Observation
<!-- id: design.industry.earth-observation -->

**Design profile:** Science  
**Operating profile:** Science  
**Product profile:** Scientific & Technical

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Earth Observation** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Earth Observation.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Satellite Imaging, Geospatial Analytics, Environmental Monitoring.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use evidence-first information architecture with strong typographic hierarchy, technical diagrams, figures, tables, and reproducible data views.
- Keep visual ornament secondary to methods, results, provenance, and source clarity.
- Use modular research cards, filters, citations, dataset tables, and figure captions.
- Choose chart types for analytical accuracy rather than visual novelty.
- Use interactive exploration when it reveals patterns that static figures cannot.
- Maintain a neutral visual system that can accommodate dense technical content without feeling institutional or dated.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- 3D charts for 2D quantitative data
- Unlabeled axes
- Dashboard decoration that competes with evidence
- Color scales without accessible legends

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Drone Delivery

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Logistics  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Drone Delivery** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Drone Delivery.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Medical Delivery, Retail Delivery, Logistics Drones.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/

- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Map-only dashboards
- Animation on continuously updating data
- Unlabeled status colors
- Oversized cards that reduce operational density

## Implementation Priority

<!-- id: design.industry.aircraft-leasing -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Aircraft Leasing** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Aircraft Leasing.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Commercial Aircraft Leasing, Private Aircraft Leasing.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Engine Manufacturing

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Engine Manufacturing** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Engine Manufacturing.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Aircraft Engines, Automotive Engines, Industrial Engines.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/

- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data

- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

# Power Electronics
<!-- id: design.industry.power-electronics -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Manufacturing  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Power Electronics** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Power Electronics.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Inverters, Converters, Power Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Oil & Gas Drilling, Mining Drilling, Water Well Drilling.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use data-rich but calm interfaces emphasizing consumption, generation, cost, reliability, and environmental performance.
- Use charts with clear units, time ranges, baselines, and comparison modes.
- Use maps for assets, service areas, projects, outages, and infrastructure where spatial context matters.
- Use technical diagrams, project photography, and process visuals rather than generic green imagery.
- Build dashboards with strong anomaly, alert, and threshold states.
- Use motion only for state change, flow visualization, and educational diagrams.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Decorative green gradients as a substitute for evidence
- Unqualified sustainability visuals
- 3D charts
- Map layers without legends

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use project- and capability-first layouts with strong grids, market/service hierarchy, project proof, bid/RFQ actions, safety/quality evidence, and controlled document access.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use real project/site photography, progress imagery, plans, BIM/technical diagrams, logistics/site context, and finished-work evidence instead of generic hard-hat stock.
- Keep schedules, project facts, bid packages, RFIs/submittals, qualifications, and document indexes highly scannable with clear status and ownership.
- Use BIM/3D, maps, phasing, or site visualization only when it improves spatial understanding, coordination, constructability, or project communication.
- Design mobile for field lookup, project contacts, plans/documents, issue capture, approvals, photos, and fast escalation rather than reproducing every desktop view.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

- Treat **RFID** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for RFID.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: RFID Tags, Tracking Systems, Asset Management.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Workplace Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Workplace Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Office Booking, Employee Experience, Hybrid Work Tools.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards
- Every surface using glassmorphism
- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Network Hardware** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Routers, Switches, Wireless Equipment.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data

- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Modern Design Strategy

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: PLM Software, Engineering Data, Product Development.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards

- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

# Customer Support Software

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Customer Support Software** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Customer Support Software.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Help Desk, Ticketing, Contact Center Software.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Map-only dashboards
- Animation on continuously updating data
- Unlabeled status colors
- Oversized cards that reduce operational density

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

# Conversational AI
<!-- id: design.industry.conversational-ai -->

**Design profile:** Ai  
**Operating profile:** Ai  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Conversational AI** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Conversational AI.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Chatbots, Voice Assistants, Customer Service AI.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Design around input → context → generation → review → action, making system state and user control explicit.
- Use conversational UI only where conversation is genuinely the best interaction model; provide structured controls for repeatable workflows.
- Separate user input, source context, AI output, citations, tool actions, and system status visually.
- Make uncertainty, limitations, provenance, and human review states legible without overwhelming the main task.
- Use streaming, progress, skeletons, and tool-call status carefully so latency feels understandable rather than mysterious.
- Use modern motion and ambient visual identity sparingly; clarity of output is more important than futuristic styling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Generic glowing-orb AI branding as the main interface
- Hiding sources or tool actions
- Typing animations that slow expert users
- Anthropomorphic UI that misrepresents autonomy

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Ad Measurement.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Audience Measurement, Campaign Measurement, Media Analytics.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use strong editorial typography, clear content hierarchy, rich metadata, and fast discovery.
- Design homepage modules around editorial priority rather than equal-card grids everywhere.
- Use sticky players, chaptering, transcripts, playlists, and save/follow controls where relevant.
- Apply motion to transitions, covers, and media states without interfering with reading.
- Use dark mode when it improves long-form or media consumption, not as a mandatory brand signal.
- Build a visual system flexible enough for breaking news, evergreen features, video, audio, and live content.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Infinite visual noise
- Autoplay audio
- Content cards with no hierarchy
- Animations that shift reading position

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Treat **Retail Analytics** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Store Analytics, Customer Analytics, Inventory Analytics.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use a product-first visual system with large, crisp imagery, restrained chrome, and strong hierarchy around price, availability, variants, and primary purchase actions.
- Favor modular card grids, comparison states, sticky purchase controls, progressive disclosure, and fast faceted navigation.
- Use editorial storytelling selectively for premium collections, launches, and category education rather than turning every page into a campaign.
- Design mobile product pages around thumb reach, sticky actions, clear variant selection, and minimal checkout friction.
- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

# FP&A
<!-- id: design.industry.fp-and-a -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **FP&A** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for FP&A.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Financial Planning, Budgeting, Forecasting.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

# Budgeting
<!-- id: design.industry.budgeting -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Budgeting** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Budgeting.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Corporate Budgeting, Personal Budgeting, Government Budgeting.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.

- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use approachable, structured learning interfaces with clear progress, next actions, and readable content.
- Design courses around modules, lessons, assessments, resources, and progress states rather than generic cards.
- Use visual hierarchy to reduce cognitive load and keep instructional content primary.
- Provide accessible calendars, deadlines, announcements, and feedback states.
- Use illustrations and motion to explain concepts, not to decorate every screen.
- For younger audiences, increase clarity and delight without reducing accessibility or information density.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
