- Gamification that obscures learning goals
- Tiny progress indicators
- Overly playful UI for serious administrative tasks
- Color-only grading/status

# AI Infrastructure
<!-- id: design.industry.ai-infrastructure -->

**Design profile:** Ai  
**Operating profile:** Ai  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **AI Infrastructure** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for AI Infrastructure.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: GPUs, Model Hosting, AI Cloud, Vector Databases.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Design around input → context → generation → review → action, making system state and user control explicit.
- Use conversational UI only where conversation is genuinely the best interaction model; provide structured controls for repeatable workflows.
- Separate user input, source context, AI output, citations, tool actions, and system status visually.
- Make uncertainty, limitations, provenance, and human review states legible without overwhelming the main task.
- Use streaming, progress, skeletons, and tool-call status carefully so latency feels understandable rather than mysterious.
- Use modern motion and ambient visual identity sparingly; clarity of output is more important than futuristic styling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Generic glowing-orb AI branding as the main interface
- Hiding sources or tool actions
- Typing animations that slow expert users
- Anthropomorphic UI that misrepresents autonomy

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

# Synthetic Media
<!-- id: design.industry.synthetic-media -->

**Design profile:** Media  
**Operating profile:** Ai  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Synthetic Media** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Synthetic Media.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: AI Video, AI Audio, Virtual Humans, Digital Avatars.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use strong editorial typography, clear content hierarchy, rich metadata, and fast discovery.
- Design homepage modules around editorial priority rather than equal-card grids everywhere.
- Use sticky players, chaptering, transcripts, playlists, and save/follow controls where relevant.
- Apply motion to transitions, covers, and media states without interfering with reading.
- Use dark mode when it improves long-form or media consumption, not as a mandatory brand signal.
- Build a visual system flexible enough for breaking news, evergreen features, video, audio, and live content.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/

- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/

- Infinite visual noise
- Autoplay audio

- Animations that shift reading position

# Facial Recognition
<!-- id: design.industry.facial-recognition -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Facial Recognition** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Facial Recognition.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Identity Verification, Security, Biometrics.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.
- Use charts and topology visuals carefully, with drill-down and textual evidence.
- Show trust evidence—controls, certifications, response process—without turning every page into a badge wall.
- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Green-code hacker clichés

- Severity conveyed by color alone
- Animated threat maps that distract from action

# Data Loss Prevention
<!-- id: design.industry.data-loss-prevention -->

**Design profile:** Events  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Data Loss Prevention** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Data Loss Prevention.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Endpoint DLP, Cloud DLP, Email DLP.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use event identity boldly while keeping date, place, agenda, registration, speakers, and ticket status immediately accessible.
- Design schedules for quick scanning, filtering, favorites, timezone handling, and mobile use.
- Use speaker/performer imagery consistently and create strong session hierarchy.
- Use motion for anticipation and transitions, not for core schedule interaction.
- Make venue maps, directions, accessibility, and check-in information event-day priorities.
- For hybrid events, integrate live status, stream access, transcripts, and replay cleanly.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **FullCalendar** — calendar, schedule, agenda, and event interfaces — https://fullcalendar.io/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Brand animation before event details
- Agenda PDFs as the only schedule
- Tiny calendar cells on mobile
- Countdown timers without real value

# Vulnerability Management
<!-- id: design.industry.vulnerability-management -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Cyber  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Vulnerability Management** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Vulnerability Management.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Vulnerability Scanning, Patch Management, Risk Prioritization.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.

# Enterprise Mobility
<!-- id: design.industry.enterprise-mobility -->

**Design profile:** Automotive  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Enterprise Mobility** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Enterprise Mobility.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Mobile Workforce, Device Management, Mobile Apps.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use immersive media, crisp spec hierarchy, model/variant comparison, and confidence-building ownership information.
- Combine editorial hero storytelling with highly functional inventory, configuration, financing, and service interfaces.
- Use dark themes selectively for performance/luxury contexts, with accessible contrast and readable forms.
- Use 3D or 360-degree product visualization for meaningful inspection and configuration.
- Keep price, availability, key specs, and primary actions continuously discoverable.
- Use motion to communicate mechanical precision, state transitions, and model changes rather than generic parallax.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Full-screen video that blocks basic information
- Dark-on-dark controls
- Overly cinematic inventory browsing
- Hiding real prices behind excessive lead forms

# Workforce Technology
<!-- id: design.industry.workforce-technology -->

**Design profile:** Software  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Workforce Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Workforce Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: HR Tech, Scheduling, Productivity, Employee Analytics.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

- Overanimated dashboards

# Outplacement
<!-- id: design.industry.outplacement -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Professional  
**Product profile:** Professional Services

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Outplacement** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Outplacement.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Career Transition, Workforce Reduction Services, Executive Career Services.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

# Employee Engagement
<!-- id: design.industry.employee-engagement -->

**Design profile:** Software  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Employee Engagement** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Employee Engagement.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Engagement Software, Employee Recognition, Workplace Surveys.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

# Billing Technology
<!-- id: design.industry.billing-technology -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Billing Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Billing Technology.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Subscription Billing, Usage Billing, Invoicing.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Reverse Logistics
<!-- id: design.industry.reverse-logistics -->

**Design profile:** Logistics  
**Operating profile:** Logistics  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Reverse Logistics** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Reverse Logistics.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Product Returns, Refurbishment, Recycling.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use operational dashboards with shipment state, ETA, exception, route, and document hierarchy.
- Combine maps with structured lists/tables so users can locate, compare, and act without relying on map interaction alone.
- Use semantic status colors with icons/text labels and explicit timestamps.
- Design high-density interfaces with sticky filters, saved views, batch actions, and drill-down drawers.
- Use live/streaming updates carefully and show last-updated time.
- Optimize mobile for drivers, field teams, proof-of-delivery, scanning, and exception handling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Leaflet** — lightweight mobile-friendly interactive maps — https://leafletjs.com/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Map-only dashboards
- Animation on continuously updating data
- Unlabeled status colors
- Oversized cards that reduce operational density

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Sanctions Screening
<!-- id: design.industry.sanctions-screening -->

**Design profile:** Security  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Sanctions Screening** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Sanctions Screening.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Financial Screening, Trade Screening, Compliance Technology.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a serious, high-contrast security design system with strong information hierarchy and minimal visual theatrics.
- For product dashboards, prioritize alert severity, asset, evidence, timeline, ownership, and remediation.
- Use dark themes only where they improve operator comfort; support light mode and accessible contrast.
- Use charts and topology visuals carefully, with drill-down and textual evidence.
- Show trust evidence—controls, certifications, response process—without turning every page into a badge wall.
- Use motion minimally; security operators value stability and speed.

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Claims Technology** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Automated Claims, Damage Assessment, Fraud Detection.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards
- Every surface using glassmorphism
- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

# Crypto Infrastructure
<!-- id: design.industry.crypto-infrastructure -->

**Design profile:** Software  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Crypto Infrastructure** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Crypto Infrastructure.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Wallet Infrastructure, Blockchain Nodes, Custody, APIs.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards
- Every surface using glassmorphism
- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

- Design mobile product pages around thumb reach, sticky actions, clear variant selection, and minimal checkout friction.
- Create visual confidence through consistent image ratios, strong whitespace, predictable controls, and transparent delivery/returns information.
- Use subtle motion for product-state changes, add-to-cart feedback, image transitions, and filters—not decorative motion that delays shopping.

# Digital Products
<!-- id: design.industry.digital-products -->

**Design profile:** Software  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Digital Products** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Digital Products.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Online Courses, Templates, E-Books, Software, Digital Downloads.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a contemporary application shell with clear workspace hierarchy, command/search affordances, contextual sidebars, and predictable state changes.
- Adopt tokenized spacing, typography, radius, elevation, and semantic colors so product and marketing surfaces share one system.
- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards
- Every surface using glassmorphism
- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Packaging Design
<!-- id: design.industry.packaging-design -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Professional  
**Product profile:** Professional Services

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Packaging Design** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Packaging Design.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Consumer Packaging, Structural Packaging, Label Design.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.

- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/

- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards
- Every surface using glassmorphism
- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

## Implementation Priority

# Enterprise AI
<!-- id: design.industry.enterprise-ai -->

**Design profile:** Ai  
**Operating profile:** Ai  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Enterprise AI** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Enterprise AI.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: AI Assistants, Automation, Analytics.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Design around input → context → generation → review → action, making system state and user control explicit.
- Use conversational UI only where conversation is genuinely the best interaction model; provide structured controls for repeatable workflows.
- Separate user input, source context, AI output, citations, tool actions, and system status visually.
- Make uncertainty, limitations, provenance, and human review states legible without overwhelming the main task.
- Use streaming, progress, skeletons, and tool-call status carefully so latency feels understandable rather than mysterious.
- Use modern motion and ambient visual identity sparingly; clarity of output is more important than futuristic styling.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Anime.js** — lightweight timelines, SVG, text, transforms, and interface animation — https://animejs.com/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Generic glowing-orb AI branding as the main interface
- Hiding sources or tool actions
- Typing animations that slow expert users
- Anthropomorphic UI that misrepresents autonomy

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Robotic Process Automation
<!-- id: design.industry.robotic-process-automation -->

**Design profile:** Industrial  
**Operating profile:** Software  
**Product profile:** Software Product

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Robotic Process Automation** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Robotic Process Automation.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Software Robots, Back-Office Automation, Enterprise Automation.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Because the Product Profile is **Software Product**, application workflow, role/permission, state, error, onboarding, search, and data-density needs take precedence over consumer-facing domain patterns. Use the domain profile for terminology, proof, visual language, and workflow context—not to invent checkout, booking, or brochure behavior.

- Use specification-first layouts with strong grids, technical hierarchy, filters, part numbers, compatibility, downloads, and RFQ actions.
- Favor durable visual language: crisp typography, neutral surfaces, high-contrast status colors, and disciplined use of brand color.
- Use technical photography, annotated diagrams, CAD/3D views, cutaways, and application imagery instead of generic lifestyle stock.
- Keep tables highly scannable with sticky headers, units, comparison states, and export/download options.
- Use 3D visualization only for configuration, fit, assembly, or spatial understanding.
- Design mobile primarily for field lookup, manuals, service, and quick contact rather than reproducing every desktop table.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **three.js** — 3D product visualization, immersive scenes, WebGL/WebGPU-oriented experiences — https://threejs.org/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Marketing-first pages that hide technical data
- Low-density tables with excessive whitespace
- Tiny specification text
- 3D effects without technical purpose

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Medical Robotics
<!-- id: design.industry.medical-robotics -->

**Design profile:** Healthcare  
**Operating profile:** Manufacturing  
**Product profile:** Operational B2B

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Medical Robotics** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Medical Robotics.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Surgical Robots, Rehabilitation Robots, Hospital Robots.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use an evidence-led, regulated-industry interface with exceptional readability, traceable claims, and clear separation of scientific, professional, procurement, and public information.
- Prioritize product/platform evidence, indications or intended use where applicable, specifications, safety information, professional resources, quality/regulatory proof, and contact/procurement actions—not assumed patient booking flows.
- Design technical and regulatory content with precise hierarchy, versioning, downloadable documents, citations, and visible status/context.
- Use authentic laboratory, manufacturing, device, professional, or care-context imagery appropriate to the actual product without implying unsupported outcomes.
- Keep safety, contraindication/warning, regulatory-status, intended-use, and escalation information visually distinct when applicable.
- Use motion minimally; prioritize credibility, evidence, performance, and accessibility.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **FullCalendar** — calendar, schedule, agenda, and event interfaces — https://fullcalendar.io/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Tiny text
- Low-contrast pastel-on-white interfaces
- Hidden emergency/contact information
- Decorative motion around sensitive tasks

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Use bento-style modularity only where cards represent real functional groups—not as decoration.
- Design empty states, onboarding, keyboard shortcuts, command palettes, and inline help as first-class product experiences.
- Use motion for continuity between states, drawers, dialogs, and layout changes while preserving speed and reduced-motion support.
- Keep documentation and product UI terminology synchronized.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Excessive nested cards
- Every surface using glassmorphism
- Invisible hover-only controls
- Overanimated dashboards

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Allied Health Education

- Treat **Allied Health Education** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.

- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Therapy Training, Technician Training, Healthcare Certification.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a calm, accessible, trust-led interface with strong readability, predictable navigation, and generous touch targets.
- Prioritize appointment, provider, location, insurance, instructions, and contact actions over decorative brand modules.
- Design forms with clear labels, step progress, save/resume behavior, inline validation, and low cognitive load.
- Use imagery that reflects real care settings and patient diversity without making unsupported outcome implications.
- Keep medical warnings, emergency guidance, and next steps visually distinct and readable.
- Use motion minimally and respect reduced-motion preferences by default.

- Decorative motion around sensitive tasks

# Education Finance
<!-- id: design.industry.education-finance -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Education Finance** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Education Finance.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Student Loans, Tuition Financing, Education Payments.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

- Use mission-led storytelling with visible evidence, impact metrics, programs, and action pathways.
- Balance emotional storytelling with transparent data and concrete outcomes.
- Create clear journeys for donate, volunteer, participate, learn, and get help.
- Use accessible campaign modules, progress indicators, and recurring-giving controls.
- Use photography ethically and avoid exploitative visual framing.
- Design impact reports and dashboards so donors can understand what changed and how resources were used.

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Emotion-only pages without evidence
- Dark patterns in donation flows
- Overly corporate dashboards on beneficiary-facing pages
- Low-contrast campaign graphics

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.

5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.

# Credit Unions
<!-- id: design.industry.credit-unions -->

**Design profile:** Finance  
**Operating profile:** Finance  
**Product profile:** Financial Experience

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Credit Unions** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Credit Unions.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Retail Finance, Cooperative Banking, Community Lending.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-trust, data-forward design system with clear numerical hierarchy, restrained color, and visible status/confirmation states.
- Keep critical balances, rates, fees, risk, and transaction states readable without relying on color alone.
- Design dense dashboards with strong grouping, predictable tables, progressive disclosure, and keyboard-operable controls.
- Use charts to answer specific financial questions; pair critical charts with values, labels, tables, and date ranges.
- Favor calm motion and immediate feedback over playful effects.
- Use explicit security and permission cues near high-impact actions without creating fear-driven visual noise.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Bootstrap 5.3** — responsive grid, forms, navigation, utilities, and common UI components — https://getbootstrap.com/
- **htmx** — HTML-first dynamic interactions without a large SPA framework — https://htmx.org/
- **Alpine.js** — lightweight client-side UI state and interactions — https://alpinejs.dev/
- **Chart.js** — accessible-minded common charts and dashboards — https://www.chartjs.org/
- **Apache ECharts** — advanced interactive charts, dashboards, large datasets, and rich visualization — https://echarts.apache.org/
- **D3** — custom data visualization and bespoke interactive graphics — https://d3js.org/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Trading-dashboard visual density on simple consumer tasks
- Red/green-only meaning
- Decorative glassmorphism over numbers
- Ambiguous transaction buttons

## Implementation Priority

1. Establish information architecture and primary user journeys.
2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.

# Clubs
<!-- id: design.industry.clubs -->

**Design profile:** Hospitality  
**Operating profile:** Hospitality  
**Product profile:** Booking & Guest

## Modern Design Strategy

- Treat **Clubs** as a distinct design domain; optimize the interface around its highest-value customer and operator tasks rather than reusing a generic template.
- Use category-specific proof, imagery, terminology, and content density so the experience immediately reads as credible for Clubs.
- Use the taxonomy's subcategories to create visual/content modules where useful: Country Clubs, Social Clubs, Private Clubs.
- Prototype the highest-risk workflow on mobile and desktop before polishing secondary marketing sections.

- Use a high-emotion editorial layer for property storytelling and a high-clarity transactional layer for rooms, rates, and policies.
- Design availability selectors, date pickers, occupancy controls, and rate cards for fast comparison.
- Use photography in consistent ratios and avoid galleries that trap users in modal loops.
- Create distinct visual hierarchy for room type, cancellation terms, included benefits, taxes, and total price.
- Use local-area maps and itinerary content to extend the property experience.
- Keep mobile booking controls sticky and reduce re-entry of dates/guests.

## Recommended Free/Open Libraries

- **Tailwind CSS** — utility-first CSS and design tokens — https://tailwindcss.com/
- **Swiper** — touch-friendly carousels, galleries, product/media sliders — https://swiperjs.com/
- **FullCalendar** — calendar, schedule, agenda, and event interfaces — https://fullcalendar.io/
- **MapLibre GL JS** — open-source GPU-accelerated vector maps, globe, 3D terrain, and data layers — https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/
- **Lucide** — consistent scalable SVG icons — https://lucide.dev/
- **Motion** — production-grade animation for HTML, SVG, React, Vue, and WebGL — https://motion.dev/

## Visual/UX Patterns to Avoid

- Brand videos before booking information
- Hidden rate conditions
- Overly decorative date pickers
- Low-contrast image overlays

## Implementation Priority

2. Define design tokens and reusable components.
3. Build accessible responsive layouts with native HTML/CSS first.
4. Add only the interaction libraries required by the workflows.
5. Add charts, maps, galleries, motion, or 3D progressively where they improve comprehension or conversion.
6. Test performance, keyboard use, touch use, reduced motion, zoom, and real content before launch.
